notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for 1 Corinthians 6, drawn from the sources I was able to access. I note at the end which traditions and views I could not reach within the tool limits.

---

## 1 Corinthians 6 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — “If any of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints!”

The opening word “Dare” (Greek *tolmaō*) is emphatic and conveys shock — Paul regards this as audacious defiance of Christian duty. Ellicott quotes Bengel: “Treason against Christians is denoted by this high-sounding word.” The lawsuits were civil disputes, not criminal cases, and were tried at the *bēma* seat in the Corinthian marketplace, where pagan onlookers would be entertained by Christians litigating against each other. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/); [PreceptAustin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-6-commentary)

“Unrighteous” (*adikos*) is used in a religious, not a moral sense — meaning “not justified before God,” i.e., unbelievers. Paul is not saying the Roman judges were necessarily corrupt (Roman law was generally sound); the scandal is that justified believers are asking the unjustified to render justice. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/); [PreceptAustin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-6-commentary)

Gill notes that even the Jewish rabbis held it a grave sin — “worse than murder” — to bring a case before Gentile courts, quoting rabbinic maxims: “he that tries a cause before the judges of the Gentiles … lo, this is an ungodly man.” — [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/6.htm)

Ellicott adds that Gentile converts, accustomed to a “proverbially litigious” society, would naturally incline toward heathen tribunals, and Paul saw this as obliterating the line between Roman jurisprudence and Christian self-sacrifice. — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

---

### v. 2 — “Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if you are to judge the world, are you not competent to judge trivial cases?”

This is the first of several “Do you not know?” questions in the chapter (also vv. 3, 9, 15, 16, 19). Paul appeals to the Corinthians’ knowledge of their future destiny: Christians will, in some sense, share in Christ’s judgment of the world (cf. Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30). This makes it absurd for them to be incapable of settling small civil disputes now. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/); [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

Ellicott sees this as referring primarily to “the conquest of the world by Christianity, which has since been accomplished,” as well as the final triumph, noting the early Church’s expectation of Christ’s near advent. — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

Gill takes a different approach: he interprets “the saints shall judge the world” as a prophecy that Christians would rise to positions of civil magistracy and governance in the world, which indeed happened within a few centuries. — [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/6.htm)

J. Vernon McGee (cited at PreceptAustin) gives three reasons Christians should judge their own matters: (1) saints will judge the world; (2) saints will judge angels; (3) the unrighteous have no place in God’s kingdom. — [PreceptAustin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-6-commentary)

---

### v. 3 — “Do you not know that we will judge angels? How much more the things of this life!”

Paul escalates the argument: not merely the world, but even angels will be judged by the saints. Guzik notes this does not mean judging faithful angels, but having a part in judging *evil* angels — a destiny that must infuriate Satan, who rebelled precisely because he refused to serve a creature he considered inferior. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

Gill interprets “judging angels” as the apostles’ ministry casting down evil spirits from their dominance over the Gentile world through the gospel, citing John 12:31 (“now shall the prince of this world be cast out”). — [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/6.htm)

Ellicott sees this as a climax of Paul’s vision of the unity of Christ and His Church triumphant — redeemed humanity will be superior to, and judges of, the spiritual world. — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

---

### v. 4 — “So if you need to settle everyday matters, do you appoint as judges those of no standing in the church?”

**This verse has a significant translation divide.** The Greek can be read as either indicative (a rhetorical question: “do you appoint…?”) or imperative (“appoint…!”). The BSB, ESV, NASB, and most modern translations read it as a question of rebuke. The KJV reads it as a command: “set them to judge who are least esteemed in the church.” — [PreceptAustin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-6-commentary)

Gill follows the imperative reading: Paul instructs them to appoint private laymen — those not in church office — as arbitrators in civil matters, rather than troubling church elders with such cases and rather than going to heathen courts. He notes the Jewish parallel of “the bench of idiots” (private persons chosen by the people to arbitrate). — [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/6.htm)

Ellicott reads it as biting sarcasm (indicative): “The very meanest of those who are to be exalted above angels … is of sufficient authority to settle such matters as you are bringing before legal tribunals.” — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

Guzik (EnduringWord) takes the indicative reading: why do you allow those “least esteemed by the church” (i.e., secular judges) to decide disputes? — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

---

### v. 5 — “I say this to your shame. Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers?”

Paul turns the sarcasm into a direct challenge. The Corinthians boasted of their “wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:18–31), yet their actions prove there is not a single wise person among them capable of arbitration. Gill notes that the Jewish custom allowed even a single approved individual to judge pecuniary cases alone. — [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/6.htm); [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

---

### v. 6 — “Instead, one brother goes to law against another, and this in front of unbelievers!”

The scandal is compounded: it is not merely lawsuits, but lawsuits *between brothers* and *before unbelievers*. The world watches Christians tear each other apart in public courts. Bridgeway Bible Commentary notes: “They shame themselves by taking Christian problems to non-Christian people for a decision.” — [Bridgeway (StudyLight)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/1-corinthians-6.html)

Paul himself was not opposed to all legal action — he appealed to Roman courts in Acts 22:25 and 25:10–11 — but he knew it was wrong when *brother goes to law against brother*. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

---

### v. 7 — “The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means that you are thoroughly defeated already. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?”

Paul says the mere existence of lawsuits between believers is already a total defeat — the Greek word (*hēttēma*) means “a failure, a shortcoming.” Ellicott renders it “a falling short of your privilege and dignity as Christians.” — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

Paul then echoes Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 5:40: it is better to suffer wrong than to defend one’s rights at the expense of God’s glory. Guzik comments: “The Corinthians were just like modern Americans: addicted to their own ‘rights.’” Paul calls the wronged party to give up what he deserves for the higher good of the Kingdom — though he adds that no one who accepts wrong for God’s glory will ultimately be a loser. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

Crucially, Paul says “why not suffer wrong *instead of bringing your dispute before unbelievers*” — not “instead of confronting the problem.” — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

---

### v. 8 — “Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, even against your own brothers!”

Far from being willing to suffer wrong, the Corinthians were actively committing wrong and defrauding each other. Paul now turns from addressing the wronged party to addressing the wrongdoer. Gill says: “neither party, not the plaintiff, nor the defendant, sought anything more or less than to wrong, trick, and defraud each other.” — [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/6.htm)

---

### vv. 9–10 — “Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God.”

Paul’s point to the cheating brother is blunt: “Do you realize what company you are keeping? The only thing you may ‘gain’ from cheating your brother is eternity with the unrighteous.” — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

The Greek terms behind “men who submit to or perform homosexual acts” are *malakoi* (literally “soft” or “effeminate,” often referring to the passive partner in male homosexual acts) and *arsenokoitai* (a compound of “male” and “bed,” referring generically to those who practice male homosexual acts). Guzik notes: “Paul did not write in or of a ‘homophobic’ culture. Homosexuality was rampant in the ancient world; 14 out of the first 15 Roman emperors were bisexual or homosexual.” — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

Gill (18th century) renders them “effeminate” and “abusers of themselves with mankind.” — [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/6.htm)

Ellicott notes the mention of gross sensual sins in connection with idolatry points to their association in pagan ritual, intensifying the danger for the Corinthians. — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

John Piper (Reformed Baptist, DesiringGod) emphasizes that these are sins which, “if you love them, cherish them, pursue them, live in them, they will destroy you — not just homosexuality or fornication.” The list includes greed, drunkenness, and reviling alongside sexual sins; no sin is singled out as uniquely damnable. — [DesiringGod](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-do-i-fight-same-sex-desires)

The phrase “will not inherit the kingdom” describes those whose lives are *characterized and dominated* by these sins, not those who commit a single act. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

---

### v. 11 — “And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”

“Such *were* some of you” — past tense. These sins should never mark a Christian’s life; if they do, immediate repentance is required. Guzik cites Gordon Fee: “Security in Christ there is, to be sure, but it is a false security that would justify sinners who have never taken seriously ‘but such were some of you.’” — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

John Piper calls this verse “the heart of biblical Christianity”: God saves homosexual and heterosexual sinners alike — those who trust Jesus are washed, sanctified, and justified. — [DesiringGod](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-marriage-be-held-in-honor/excerpts/sexual-desires-do-not-define-you)

Three works of God are listed: (1) **Washed** — cleansed from sin by Christ’s blood and God’s Word (Titus 3:5; Ephesians 5:26); (2) **Sanctified** — set apart for God; (3) **Justified** — declared righteous before God’s court. Paul lists all three Persons of the Trinity in connection with this work (“Lord Jesus Christ…Spirit of our God”). — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

Ellicott notes the unusual order: sanctified before justified, which is not the theological sequence — here “sanctified” means being made holy, not gradual growth in holiness. The washing refers to baptism as a voluntary act (Acts 22:16). — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

---

### v. 12 — “‘Everything is permissible for me,’ but not everything is beneficial. ‘Everything is permissible for me,’ but I will not be mastered by anything.”

Paul now pivots from lawsuits to sexual purity. This was probably a slogan Paul himself had used in teaching about Christian liberty (cf. Colossians 2:16–17), but the Corinthians had twisted it into a license for sin — specifically, using prostitutes. Paul repeats the slogan but adds two crucial limits: (1) not everything is *beneficial* (profitable); (2) the believer must not be *mastered* or brought under the power of anything. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

Ellicott highlights a verbal play in the Greek: “All things are lawful (*exesti*) for me, but I will not be brought under the power (*exousiasthēsomai*) of any” — there is such a thing as becoming the slave of liberty itself. — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

---

### v. 13 — “‘Food for the stomach and the stomach for food,’ but God will destroy them both. The body is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.”

The Corinthians apparently used the slogan “food for the stomach and the stomach for food” to justify sexual indulgence: “My body wants food, so I eat. My body wants sex, so I hire a prostitute.” Paul rejects the parallel: the stomach and food are temporary — God will destroy both. But the body is for the Lord, and the Lord is for the body. The body, unlike the digestive system, is destined for resurrection and belongs to Christ. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

Ellicott provides a formal argument structure: (a) Meats only affect the organ designed for them; (b) Meats and that organ perish together — therefore eating is an indifferent matter. But (a) Fornication affects the whole person; (b) The person is immortal — therefore fornication is *not* an indifferent matter. — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

---

### v. 14 — “By His power God raised the Lord from the dead, and He will raise us also.”

The resurrection of the body gives weight to sexual ethics. What we do with our bodies matters eternally, because our bodies will be raised. Ellicott notes this is one of the few verses showing Paul did not necessarily assume Christ would return within his own lifetime. — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

---

### vv. 15–16 — “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never! Or don’t you know that he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body? For it is said, ‘The two will become one flesh.’”

The argument intensifies: the believer’s body is a *member of Christ*. Sexual union with a prostitute therefore drags a member of Christ into that union — an unthinkable contradiction. Guzik says: “Paul reacts to this in the most negative way possible in the Greek language: *mē genoito* — ‘May it never be!’” — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

Paul applies Genesis 2:24 (“the two will become one flesh”) to sex outside marriage: even in casual encounters, a genuine “one flesh” union occurs — but under God’s curse rather than blessing. Guzik comments: “In the Biblical understanding of sex, there is no such thing as ‘casual sex.’” — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

---

### v. 17 — “But he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit.”

The believer’s spiritual union with Christ stands in direct opposition to physical union with a prostitute. The deep human longings for love, acceptance, and adventure that drive lust are ultimately satisfied — far more completely — in union with the Lord. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

---

### v. 18 — “Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a man can commit is outside his body, but he who sins sexually sins against his own body.”

The command is “flee,” not “resist” or “reason with.” Guzik points to Joseph (Genesis 39:7–21) as the model — he ran even when it cost him. He quotes Adam Clarke: “Some sins, or solicitations to sin, may be reasoned with; in the above cases, if you parley you are undone; reason not, but FLY!” — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

“Sins against his own body”: Paul does not say sexual sin is *worse* than other sins, but that it has a unique effect on the body — physical, moral, and spiritual. GotQuestions notes that some Greek-influenced Corinthians believed the body was unimportant or evil; Paul counters that sexual immorality uniquely defiles the body, which belongs to the Lord. — [GotQuestions (search excerpt)](https://www.gotquestions.org/sin-against-your-own-body.html)

Ellicott compares the body to a temple: other sins may profane outer courts; this sin penetrates the holy of holies. He quotes the Litany: “From fornication, and all other deadly sin, good Lord, deliver us.” — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

---

### vv. 19–20 — “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.”

The climax of Paul’s argument: the individual believer’s body is a temple (Greek *naos* — the inner sanctuary) of the Holy Spirit. This gives two reasons we are not our own: (1) the indwelling Spirit is given by God, and (2) we were “bought at a price” — the blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19). Both truths forbid sexual immorality. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)

Ellicott notes that the words “and in your spirit” found in the KJV are absent from the older Greek manuscripts; they were likely added later for verbal completeness, but actually weaken Paul’s point — the dignity of the *body* is his sole theme here. — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

John Piper summarizes: “God bought your body. You are not your own. Therefore, glorify God in your body.” The body is not a disposable shell; it is God’s purchased possession and dwelling place. — [DesiringGod](https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/god-bought-your-body)

---

## Denominational Distinctives & Differing Views

### Notable Textual/Interpretive Difference

**v. 4** — Imperative vs. Indicative: The KJV and Gill (older Baptist) read it as a command (“set them to judge” — appoint the lowliest church members as arbitrators). Modern translations (ESV, NASB, BSB, NIV) and Ellicott read it as a sarcastic question (“do you appoint…?”). This reflects a genuine grammatical ambiguity in the Greek. — [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/6.htm); [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

### On “judging angels” (v. 3)
- **Gill (Baptist):** interprets it as the apostolic ministry casting down evil spirits from Gentile dominance. — [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_corinthians/6.htm)
- **Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** sees it as the future eschatological role of believers in judging fallen angels at the final judgment. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** sees it as the climactic expression of the Church’s triumph in union with Christ, not a literal courtroom scene. — [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/6.htm)

### On v. 9 (homosexual terms)
- **Guzik / EnduringWord (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** *malakoi* = male prostitutes (passive partners); *arsenokoitai* = all homosexual practice. Context shows Paul was not only condemning temple prostitution but all homosexual acts. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/)
- **John Piper (Reformed Baptist):** both homosexual and heterosexual sinners are condemned under these categories, but verse 11 shows that God saves people from both and transforms them. Same-sex attraction may not entirely vanish, but sanctification “swallows up” disordered desires in something greater. — [DesiringGod](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-marriage-be-held-in-honor/excerpts/sexual-desires-do-not-define-you)

### On v. 7 (lawsuits)
The traditional Protestant consensus (spanning Guzik, McGee, GotQuestions, Bridgeway) is unanimous: Christians should never sue fellow Christians in secular courts. The distinction is drawn between criminal matters (which belong to the state, Romans 13) and civil disputes between believers. Paul’s own appeal to Caesar (Acts 25) shows using secular courts is permissible when dealing with unbelievers or criminal charges. — [EnduringWord](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-6/); [PreceptAustin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-6-commentary)
